coding_mcq.title: Worst-Case Time Complexity of QuickSort
coding_mcq.question: What is the worst-case time complexity of QuickSort when using the standard last-element partitioning scheme?
coding_mcq.explanation: QuickSort degrades to O(N^2) in the worst case when the array is already sorted (or reverse-sorted) and the pivot chosen is always the maximum or minimum element, producing completely unbalanced partitions of size 0 and N-1.

coding_mcq.title: Balanced Binary Search Tree Lookup
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity to search for an element in a balanced Binary Search Tree (AVL or Red-Black Tree) with N nodes?
coding_mcq.explanation: In a self-balancing BST, the height is strictly maintained at O(log N). Searching involves following one branch from root to leaf, taking O(log N) comparisons.

coding_mcq.title: Cycle Detection in Linked List
coding_mcq.question: Floyd's Cycle-Finding Algorithm (Tortoise and Hare) detects a cycle in a linked list using which auxiliary space complexity?
coding_mcq.explanation: Floyd's algorithm uses two pointers (slow moving 1 step and fast moving 2 steps). Since it only requires two pointer variables regardless of list length, the auxiliary space complexity is strictly O(1).

coding_mcq.title: Queue Implementation using Stacks
coding_mcq.question: When implementing a FIFO Queue using two LIFO Stacks, what is the amortized time complexity of the dequeue operation?
coding_mcq.explanation: While a single dequeue might occasionally take O(N) when transferring elements from the input stack to the output stack, every element is pushed and popped from each stack exactly twice across its lifetime, yielding an amortized O(1) time per operation.

coding_mcq.title: Stable Sorting Algorithms
coding_mcq.question: Which of the following sorting algorithms is inherently stable in its standard implementation?
coding_mcq.explanation: MergeSort is stable because when two elements have equal keys, the element from the left sub-array is chosen first (using <=), preserving their original relative order. QuickSort, HeapSort, and SelectionSort are unstable in their standard forms.

coding_mcq.title: Heap Construction Time Complexity
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity to build a binary heap from an unsorted array of N elements using the bottom-up heapify algorithm?
coding_mcq.explanation: Building a heap from an array bottom-up takes linear time O(N), not O(N log N). This is because nodes at lower levels have shorter paths to the bottom; mathematically, sum_{h=0}^{log N} (N / 2^(h+1)) * O(h) converges to O(N).

coding_mcq.title: Hash Table Collision Resolution
coding_mcq.question: What is the worst-case search time complexity in a Hash Table with N elements if all keys hash to the same bucket (using separate chaining)?
coding_mcq.explanation: If all N keys collide in the same bucket, all elements reside in a single linked list, reducing lookup to a linear traversal taking O(N) time.

coding_mcq.title: Shortest Path with Negative Edge Weights
coding_mcq.question: Which single-source shortest path algorithm can handle graphs containing negative edge weights and detect negative cycles?
coding_mcq.explanation: The Bellman-Ford algorithm relaxes all edges V-1 times and can correctly handle negative edge weights as well as detect reachable negative weight cycles. Dijkstra's greedy choice assumption fails with negative edges.

coding_mcq.title: Minimum Spanning Tree Algorithms
coding_mcq.question: Which data structure is typically used to optimize Kruskal's algorithm to achieve O(E log V) or O(E alpha(V)) edge processing?
coding_mcq.explanation: Kruskal's algorithm sorts all edges by weight and uses a Disjoint Set Union (DSU with union by rank and path compression) to quickly determine if adding an edge forms a cycle in near-constant O(alpha(V)) time.

coding_mcq.title: In-order Traversal of BST
coding_mcq.question: What sequence of values is produced when performing an In-Order traversal (Left, Root, Right) on a valid Binary Search Tree?
coding_mcq.explanation: In a BST, all left descendants are smaller than the node, and all right descendants are larger. Traversing Left -> Root -> Right visits nodes in strictly ascending (sorted) order.

coding_mcq.title: 0/1 Knapsack Dynamic Programming
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity of solving the 0/1 Knapsack problem with N items and maximum weight capacity W using Dynamic Programming?
coding_mcq.explanation: The 2D dynamic programming table has (N+1) rows and (W+1) columns, where each cell is computed in O(1) time, resulting in O(N * W) pseudo-polynomial time complexity.

coding_mcq.title: B-Tree Node Properties
coding_mcq.question: In a B-Tree of order M, what is the maximum number of children any internal node can have?
coding_mcq.explanation: By definition, a B-Tree of order M can have at most M children (and at most M-1 keys) in any node. Internal nodes (except root) must have at least ceil(M/2) children.

coding_mcq.title: Stack applications
coding_mcq.question: Which of the following problems is most naturally solved using a Monotonic Stack?
options: Finding shortest path in unweighted graph
Next Greater Element for each array item
Generating all permutations of a string
coding_mcq.explanation: A monotonic stack maintains elements in sorted order and finds the Next Greater Element (or Previous Greater Element) in linear O(N) time by pushing elements and popping smaller ones.

coding_mcq.title: Trie (Prefix Tree) Lookup
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity to search for a word of length L in a Trie containing N total words?
coding_mcq.explanation: In a Trie, search is independent of the number of words N stored in the dictionary. It solely depends on the length of the query word L, requiring exactly O(L) pointer transitions.

coding_mcq.title: Space Complexity of Recursive Fibonacci
coding_mcq.question: What is the auxiliary space complexity (call stack depth) of naive recursive Fibonacci: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)?
coding_mcq.explanation: Even though the naive recursive Fibonacci generates O(2^N) calls in total time, the call stack depth only reaches N at any given time (one branch down to base case), resulting in O(N) maximum stack space.

coding_mcq.title: Deadlock Conditions
coding_mcq.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Coffman's four necessary conditions for a deadlock to occur?
coding_mcq.explanation: The four Coffman conditions are: Mutual Exclusion, Hold and Wait, No Preemption, and Circular Wait. If preemption is allowed (resources can be forcibly taken away), deadlock cannot occur.

coding_mcq.title: Process vs Thread Memory
coding_mcq.question: Which of the following is uniquely private to each thread within the same process (not shared with peer threads)?
coding_mcq.explanation: Threads within the same process share code, global variables, heap, and open file descriptors. However, each thread maintains its own Program Counter (PC), CPU registers, and call stack to execute independent call paths.

coding_mcq.title: Virtual Memory and Thrashing
coding_mcq.question: What causes 'Thrashing' in an operating system?
options: A high rate of network packet collisions
The OS spending more time swapping pages in and out of disk than executing user instructions
Multiple processes simultaneously deadlocking on mutex locks
coding_mcq.explanation: Thrashing occurs when the total working set of active processes exceeds physical memory. The OS constantly replaces pages that are needed immediately, causing continuous disk I/O page faults and near-zero CPU utilization.

coding_mcq.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
coding_mcq.question: What is the primary function of a Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) in modern computer architectures?
options: Buffering disk writes before writing to blocks
A high-speed hardware cache that stores recent virtual-to-physical page translations
A queue for preempted threads waiting for CPU time
A register holding interrupt vector tables
coding_mcq.explanation: The TLB is an associative hardware cache inside the MMU that caches recent virtual page number to physical frame number mappings, avoiding slow multi-level page table traversals in RAM.

coding_mcq.title: CPU Scheduling Algorithms
coding_mcq.question: Which CPU scheduling algorithm gives the minimum average waiting time for a given set of processes?
coding_mcq.explanation: Shortest Job First (SJF) is mathematically provably optimal in terms of minimizing average waiting time because scheduling shorter jobs first minimizes the delay experienced by all subsequent jobs.

coding_mcq.title: Fork System Call
coding_mcq.question: In Unix-like systems, what does the fork() system call return to the newly created child process upon success?
options: The Process ID (PID) of the parent
coding_mcq.explanation: Upon successful execution, fork() returns the child's PID to the parent process and returns 0 to the child process. A negative value indicates failure.

coding_mcq.title: Counting Semaphore vs Binary Semaphore
coding_mcq.question: If a counting semaphore is initialized to 5, and 8 wait() (P) operations and 5 signal() (V) operations are executed, what is the final value?
coding_mcq.explanation: Initial value = 5. Each wait() decrements the count by 1 (-8) and each signal() increments it by 1 (+5). Final value = 5 - 8 + 5 = 2.

coding_mcq.title: Demand Paging and Page Fault
coding_mcq.question: When is a 'Page Fault' interrupt generated by the Memory Management Unit (MMU)?
options: When an accessed virtual page is not currently mapped into physical RAM (valid-invalid bit is 0)
When the CPU executes an invalid instruction opcode
When two threads simultaneously write to shared memory
coding_mcq.explanation: A page fault occurs when a program tries to access an address on a virtual page that has not yet been loaded into a physical memory frame (its valid bit in the page table is false).

coding_mcq.title: Belady's Anomaly
coding_mcq.question: Belady's Anomaly is a phenomenon where increasing the number of page frames results in an increase in page faults. Which page replacement algorithm exhibits this anomaly?
coding_mcq.explanation: FIFO exhibits Belady's anomaly because it does not belong to the class of stack algorithms (where the set of pages in memory for n frames is always a subset of pages for n+1 frames). LRU and OPT are immune to Belady's anomaly.

coding_mcq.title: Context Switching Overhead
coding_mcq.question: Why does context switching between processes incur a higher performance overhead than context switching between threads of the same process?
options: Process context switching requires switching virtual address spaces, invalidating TLB entries and CPU caches
Threads do not use CPU registers
Processes run in kernel mode while threads run in user mode
coding_mcq.explanation: Context switching between processes requires changing memory page tables (updating CR3 register), which flushes or invalidates TLB entries and leads to cache misses. Threads in the same process share the same address space, avoiding TLB invalidation.

coding_mcq.title: Banker's Algorithm
coding_mcq.question: What is the primary objective of the Banker's Algorithm in an operating system?
coding_mcq.explanation: The Banker's Algorithm is a Deadlock Avoidance algorithm. It evaluates resource allocation requests dynamically by checking whether granting the request keeps the system in a 'Safe State' where at least one execution sequence can finish.

coding_mcq.title: Critical Section Problem
coding_mcq.question: Which three requirements must any valid solution to the Critical Section problem satisfy?
coding_mcq.explanation: Any classic solution to the Critical Section problem must satisfy: 1) Mutual Exclusion (only one process at a time in critical section), 2) Progress (selection of next process cannot be postponed indefinitely), and 3) Bounded Waiting (limit on times other processes enter before a request is granted).

coding_mcq.title: OSI Model Transport Layer
coding_mcq.question: Which layer of the OSI reference model is responsible for end-to-end communication, flow control, error recovery, and port addressing?
coding_mcq.explanation: The Transport Layer (Layer 4) provides transparent transfer of data between end users, handling end-to-end reliability, flow control, segmentation, and port addressing (TCP and UDP).

coding_mcq.title: TCP 3-Way Handshake
coding_mcq.question: What is the correct sequence of TCP flag packets exchanged during a standard TCP connection establishment?
coding_mcq.explanation: The 3-way handshake begins with client sending SYN, server replying with SYN-ACK (synchronize sequence numbers and acknowledge client's SYN), and client responding with ACK to confirm the connection.

coding_mcq.title: HTTP Status Code 503
coding_mcq.question: What does an HTTP 503 status code response from a web server signify?
options: Service Unavailable (Server temporarily overloaded or under maintenance)
coding_mcq.explanation: HTTP 503 Service Unavailable indicates that the server is currently unable to handle the incoming request due to a temporary overloading or scheduled maintenance.

coding_mcq.title: DNS Resolution Protocol
coding_mcq.question: By default, which transport layer protocol and port number does standard DNS query resolution use for name lookups?
coding_mcq.explanation: Standard DNS client queries use UDP on port 53 because UDP is lightweight, stateless, and fast without the overhead of connection setup. DNS switches to TCP port 53 for zone transfers or responses exceeding 512 bytes.

coding_mcq.title: Subnet Mask and Host Capacity
coding_mcq.question: How many usable host IP addresses are available in a subnetwork with the CIDR prefix /28?
coding_mcq.explanation: A /28 subnet has 32 - 28 = 4 host bits. Total addresses = 2^4 = 16. Subtracting 2 reserved addresses (one for the network address and one for the broadcast address) yields 14 usable host IPs.

coding_mcq.title: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
coding_mcq.question: What is the primary function of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)?
options: Resolving a domain name (URL) into an IP address
Translating an IP address (Network Layer) into a physical MAC address (Data Link Layer)
Assigning dynamic IP addresses to new network clients
coding_mcq.explanation: ARP operates between the Data Link Layer and Network Layer to map a known 32-bit IPv4 address to a 48-bit physical MAC address on a local area network.

coding_mcq.title: TCP vs UDP Reliability
coding_mcq.question: Which of the following characteristics accurately differentiates UDP from TCP?
options: UDP guarantees in-order delivery of packets
UDP is connectionless, has minimal header overhead (8 bytes), and provides no built-in retransmissions
UDP establishes a 3-way handshake before transmitting data
coding_mcq.explanation: UDP is connectionless and lightweight with an 8-byte header (compared to TCP's 20-60 bytes). It sends datagrams without establishing a handshake and does not guarantee ordering or retransmissions, making it ideal for streaming and gaming.

coding_mcq.title: TCP Congestion Control Mechanisms
coding_mcq.question: In TCP Tahoe/Reno, what action is taken when a packet loss is detected via a Retransmission Timeout (RTO)?
options: Congestion Window (cwnd) is set to 1 MSS and slow start begins
Slow Start Threshold (ssthresh) is set to infinity
coding_mcq.explanation: When an RTO occurs (a severe indicator of congestion), TCP sets ssthresh to half of the current cwnd, resets cwnd to 1 Maximum Segment Size (MSS), and drops back into the Slow Start phase.

coding_mcq.title: Distance Vector Routing Protocol
coding_mcq.question: The 'Count-to-Infinity' problem is a well-known vulnerability associated with which type of routing algorithm?
coding_mcq.explanation: The Count-to-Infinity problem occurs in Distance-Vector routing (like RIP based on Bellman-Ford) when routing loops cause two or more nodes to continuously update and increment their metric toward an unreachable destination up to infinity (or 16 in RIP).

coding_mcq.title: HTTPS and TLS Handshake
coding_mcq.question: How does HTTPS achieve secure data transmission while maintaining high processing performance?
options: It uses asymmetric encryption (RSA/ECC) for all payload data throughout the entire session
It uses asymmetric encryption during the TLS handshake to exchange a symmetric session key, then uses fast symmetric encryption (AES) for payload transfer
It transmits data via plain text but verifies with digital signatures
It switches between HTTP and FTP dynamically
coding_mcq.explanation: Asymmetric public-key cryptography is computationally expensive. HTTPS uses asymmetric cryptography only during the initial TLS handshake to authenticate the server and securely agree upon a shared secret, which is then used with fast symmetric encryption (like AES-GCM) for the bulk data transfer.

coding_mcq.title: ACID Properties - Isolation
coding_mcq.question: In relational database ACID properties, what does 'Isolation' guarantee?
options: Transactions survive power failures through write-ahead logging
Concurrent execution of transactions leaves the database in the same state as if they were executed sequentially
All operations within a transaction complete or none do
Data complies with all integrity constraints
coding_mcq.explanation: Isolation ensures that concurrent transactions do not interfere with or observe uncommitted intermediate states of each other. The result is equivalent to some serial execution schedule.

coding_mcq.title: Database Normalization - BCNF
coding_mcq.question: A relational table is in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) if and only if for every non-trivial functional dependency X -> Y:
options: Y is a subset of X
coding_mcq.explanation: A relation is in BCNF if for every functional dependency X -> Y, X is a superkey of the relation. This eliminates all redundancy based on functional dependencies.

coding_mcq.title: B+ Tree Indexing in Databases
coding_mcq.question: Why do modern database engines (such as MySQL InnoDB and PostgreSQL) utilize B+ Trees instead of standard B-Trees for disk indexing?
options: B+ Trees hold duplicate keys at all levels
All records/data pointers reside exclusively in the leaf nodes, which are linked sequentially to enable efficient range scans
B+ Trees have a smaller fan-out factor
B+ Trees do not require rebalancing during deletions
coding_mcq.explanation: In a B+ Tree, non-leaf nodes contain only keys (routing pointers), maximizing branching factor (fan-out) and reducing tree height. All actual records or data pointers are stored in leaf nodes, which are chained into a doubly linked list, enabling extremely fast sequential range queries.

coding_mcq.title: SQL Joins - Left Outer Join
coding_mcq.question: What does a LEFT OUTER JOIN between Table A and Table B return?
options: Only matching records present in both Table A and Table B
All records from Table A, along with matching records from Table B (with NULLs for unmatched Table B rows)
All records from Table B with matching records from Table A
A cartesian cross product of Table A and Table B
coding_mcq.explanation: A LEFT OUTER JOIN preserves every row from the left table (Table A). When a matching row exists in Table B based on the join predicate, values are combined; when no match exists, NULL values are filled for Table B columns.

coding_mcq.title: Database Transaction Isolation Levels
coding_mcq.question: Which transaction isolation level prevents 'Dirty Reads' and 'Non-Repeatable Reads', but may still permit 'Phantom Reads' in standard ANSI SQL?
coding_mcq.explanation: Under Repeatable Read, shared locks prevent other transactions from modifying rows read by the current transaction (avoiding dirty reads and non-repeatable reads). However, insert operations adding new matching rows ('phantoms') are still possible unless range locks (Serializable) are used.

coding_mcq.title: Primary Key vs Candidate Key
coding_mcq.question: What is the relationship between a Candidate Key and a Primary Key in a relational table?
options: A Candidate Key is always composed of foreign keys
A Primary Key is chosen from the set of minimal Candidate Keys to uniquely identify tuples, and cannot contain NULL values
A table can have multiple Primary Keys but only one Candidate Key
Primary keys allow NULL values while Candidate keys do not
coding_mcq.explanation: A candidate key is a minimal superkey that uniquely identifies a row. The database designer selects one of these candidate keys to serve as the Primary Key. Unlike candidate keys which may allow nulls under some engines, primary keys strictly disallow NULL.

coding_mcq.title: SQL GROUP BY and HAVING Clause
coding_mcq.question: What is the key difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause in an SQL statement?
options: WHERE filters groups after aggregation, while HAVING filters individual rows before aggregation
WHERE filters rows before aggregation, while HAVING filters groups after aggregate functions (e.g., COUNT, SUM, AVG) are applied
WHERE and HAVING are completely interchangeable synonyms
HAVING can only be used with SELECT * statements
coding_mcq.explanation: The WHERE clause filters individual rows before they are grouped. The HAVING clause applies filters to grouped summaries after aggregate calculations (such as HAVING COUNT(*) > 5).

coding_mcq.title: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
coding_mcq.question: In database concurrency control, what does the Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol guarantee?
coding_mcq.explanation: Two-Phase Locking (Growing phase where locks are acquired, Shrinking phase where locks are released) guarantees conflict serializability of concurrent execution schedules. However, basic 2PL does NOT prevent deadlocks.

coding_mcq.title: Polymorphism: Compile-Time vs Run-Time
coding_mcq.question: Which mechanism exemplifies dynamic (run-time) polymorphism in object-oriented programming?
coding_mcq.explanation: Method Overriding achieves run-time polymorphism by dispatching method calls dynamically at execution time based on the actual object type (via virtual method tables / vtables), whereas overloading is resolved at compile time.

coding_mcq.title: Abstract Class vs Interface
coding_mcq.question: What is a distinguishing characteristic of an Abstract Class compared to an Interface in Java/C++?
options: An abstract class can declare instance variables and concrete constructor implementations to hold state, whereas pure interfaces define only behavior contracts
A class can extend multiple abstract classes
Interfaces can instantiate direct objects using the 'new' keyword
Abstract classes cannot contain any implemented methods
coding_mcq.explanation: Abstract classes can maintain state (instance fields) and constructors, representing an 'is-a' inheritance relationship. In contrast, interfaces represent 'can-do' contracts. (In Java 8+, interfaces can provide default methods, but cannot maintain state instance fields).

coding_mcq.title: The Diamond Problem in Inheritance
coding_mcq.question: How does C++ resolve the 'Diamond Problem' of multiple inheritance where a class inherits from two classes that share a common base?
coding_mcq.explanation: Virtual inheritance in C++ (e.g., `class B : virtual public A`) ensures that only one shared subobject of base class A exists in the most derived class, resolving ambiguity.

coding_mcq.title: SOLID Principles - Open/Closed Principle
coding_mcq.question: According to the Open/Closed Principle (the 'O' in SOLID), software entities should be:
options: Open to modification, closed to extension
Open for extension, but closed for modification
Open source and closed to proprietary licensing
Open to all subclasses, closed to unit tests
coding_mcq.explanation: The Open/Closed Principle states that classes, modules, and functions should be open for extension (their behavior can be extended without changing their source code) and closed for modification (existing verified code is not altered).

coding_mcq.title: Singleton Design Pattern
coding_mcq.question: What is the purpose of the 'volatile' keyword when implementing the Double-Checked Locking pattern in a thread-safe Singleton in Java?
options: It speeds up garbage collection of the instance
It prevents compiler and CPU instruction reordering during instance construction
It allows the instance to be cloned across threads
It serializes the object to disk
coding_mcq.explanation: Without the `volatile` modifier, the JVM or CPU can reorder instructions during `instance = new Singleton()`, assigning memory to the reference before the constructor finishes executing, allowing another thread to observe a partially-initialized object.

coding_mcq.title: Depth First Search (DFS) Implementation
coding_mcq.question: Which abstract data structure is fundamentally utilized to implement Depth First Search (DFS) iteratively on a graph?
coding_mcq.explanation: DFS traverses deep into a graph branch before backtracking, which inherently follows Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) order, naturally managed by a Stack (or the call stack in recursion).

coding_mcq.title: Breadth First Search (BFS) Implementation
coding_mcq.question: Which data structure is fundamentally required to implement Breadth First Search (BFS) level-order traversal on a graph?
coding_mcq.explanation: BFS explores nodes level-by-level in First-In-First-Out (FIFO) sequence, requiring a Queue to store discovered vertices.

coding_mcq.title: Circular Queue Full Condition
coding_mcq.question: In an array of capacity N implementing a Circular Queue with front and rear indices, what is the standard condition indicating the queue is full?
coding_mcq.explanation: In a circular queue of size N with circular wraparound, the queue is full when advancing rear by one modulo N brings it to the front index: (rear + 1) % N == front.

coding_mcq.title: Postfix Expression Evaluation
coding_mcq.question: What is the evaluated result of the postfix expression: 6 3 2 + * 5 - ?
coding_mcq.explanation: Step 1: 3 and 2 are added (3 + 2 = 5). Step 2: 6 and 5 are multiplied (6 * 5 = 30). Step 3: 5 is subtracted (30 - 5 = 25).

coding_mcq.title: Binary Tree Maximum Nodes at Depth D
coding_mcq.question: What is the maximum number of nodes possible at level (depth) L of a binary tree, assuming the root is at level 0?
coding_mcq.explanation: Level 0 has at most 2^0 = 1 node (root), level 1 has 2^1 = 2, level 2 has 2^2 = 4, and level L has at most 2^L nodes.

coding_mcq.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm Limitations
coding_mcq.question: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm fail to produce correct shortest paths on graphs with negative edge weights?
options: Its greedy assumption that visiting a node guarantees the finalized shortest distance is violated when a future negative edge can decrease path cost
It requires graphs to be acyclic
It only works on directed graphs
coding_mcq.explanation: Dijkstra's algorithm greedily assumes that once a node is marked visited with minimum distance, its shortest distance cannot be improved. A negative edge can retroactively lower an already finalized distance, breaking the algorithm.

coding_mcq.title: Dynamic Programming: Memoization vs Tabulation
coding_mcq.question: How does Top-Down Dynamic Programming (Memoization) fundamentally differ from Bottom-Up Dynamic Programming (Tabulation)?
options: Memoization is iterative while Tabulation is recursive
Memoization uses recursion and caches subproblem results as they are called, while Tabulation solves subproblems iteratively starting from base cases
Memoization cannot be used for the Knapsack problem
coding_mcq.explanation: Top-Down with Memoization preserves the recursive formulation and caches answers on-demand. Bottom-Up with Tabulation builds an iterative table starting from base cases up to the desired target.

coding_mcq.title: AVL Tree Balance Factor
coding_mcq.question: In an AVL tree, what are the allowed values for the balance factor (Height(Left) - Height(Right)) of any node?
coding_mcq.explanation: An AVL tree is strictly balanced: the height difference between the left and right subtrees of any node cannot exceed 1, meaning the balance factor must be in {-1, 0, +1}.

coding_mcq.title: Linear Probing Primary Clustering
coding_mcq.question: What is 'Primary Clustering' in open-addressing hash tables using Linear Probing?
options: A cluster of servers sharing a hash ring
Tendency for occupied slots to form contiguous blocks, increasing search and insertion times for neighboring keys
Duplication of hash values in a secondary cache
coding_mcq.explanation: In linear probing, when collisions occur, keys are placed in adjacent slots. Once a contiguous block of filled slots forms, any key that hashes into the block is forced to the end of the block, making it grow even larger.

coding_mcq.title: Topological Sorting Condition
coding_mcq.question: Topological sorting can be performed on which type of graph?
coding_mcq.explanation: A topological sort produces a linear ordering of vertices such that for every directed edge u -> v, u comes before v. This is only possible if the graph has directed edges and NO cycles (a DAG).

coding_mcq.title: OS System Calls vs Library Functions
coding_mcq.question: What hardware mechanism transitions the CPU from User Mode to Kernel Mode during a system call execution?
coding_mcq.explanation: A system call executes a software interrupt (trap instruction like 'syscall' or 'int 0x80') that causes the CPU to switch privilege levels from user mode (Ring 3) to kernel mode (Ring 0) and branch to the kernel's interrupt service routine.

coding_mcq.title: Inodes in Unix File Systems
coding_mcq.question: Which piece of information is NOT stored inside an Inode in a standard Unix file system?
coding_mcq.explanation: An Inode stores file metadata (size, owner, permissions, timestamps, data block pointers). The actual file name is stored in directory entry files (dentry), which map file names to inode numbers.

coding_mcq.title: Zombie Process in Unix
coding_mcq.question: What is a 'Zombie Process' in Unix-like operating systems?
options: A process running in an infinite loop consuming 100% CPU
A process that has finished execution but still has an entry in the process table because its parent has not yet read its exit status via wait()
A process whose parent terminated, leaving it adopted by init
A process swapped out to disk indefinitely
coding_mcq.explanation: A zombie process has completed execution via exit(), but its entry remains in the process table so its parent process can read its return code using wait(). Once the parent calls wait(), the zombie entry is released.

coding_mcq.title: Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
coding_mcq.question: Which Inter-Process Communication (IPC) mechanism provides the fastest data exchange between processes on the same machine?
coding_mcq.explanation: Shared Memory is the fastest IPC mechanism because once the memory region is mapped into the address spaces of the participating processes, data can be accessed directly without kernel intervention or data copying.

coding_mcq.title: Spooling in Operating Systems
coding_mcq.question: What does SPOOLing stand for, and what is its primary use in operating systems?
options: Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line; used to buffer I/O data for slow devices like printers
Serial Port Output Online Loading; used for network card communication
Synchronized Process Operating Online; used for thread synchronization
System Performance Optimization On Linux; used for disk defragmentation
coding_mcq.explanation: SPOOLing (Simultaneous Peripheral Operations On-Line) intercepts data intended for a slow peripheral (like a printer) and buffers it on a fast intermediate storage (disk) so the CPU does not wait for the slow device.

coding_mcq.title: Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU)
coding_mcq.question: What is the standard Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) size for an Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) frame payload at Layer 3?
coding_mcq.explanation: The standard Ethernet MTU is 1500 bytes. IP packets larger than 1500 bytes must be fragmented into smaller packets unless Jumbo Frames are configured.

coding_mcq.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP)
coding_mcq.question: What are the four phases of the DHCP lease handshake (DORA process)?
coding_mcq.explanation: The DHCP DORA process consists of: DHCP Discover (broadcast by client), DHCP Offer (unicast/broadcast by server), DHCP Request (client requests offered IP), and DHCP Acknowledge (server confirms lease).

coding_mcq.title: IPv4 vs IPv6 Address Length
coding_mcq.question: What are the exact bit lengths of an IPv4 address and an IPv6 address respectively?
coding_mcq.explanation: IPv4 uses 32 bits (4 octets, providing ~4.3 billion addresses), while IPv6 uses 128 bits (16 octets, represented as 8 groups of 4 hexadecimal digits, providing 2^128 addresses).

coding_mcq.title: TCP FIN vs RST Flags
coding_mcq.question: What is the difference between a TCP FIN flag and a TCP RST flag?
options: FIN initiates a graceful 4-way connection teardown, whereas RST immediately aborts and terminates the connection forcefully
FIN resets sequence numbers while RST finalizes encryption
RST is only sent by clients, FIN only by servers
FIN is used in UDP, RST is used in TCP
coding_mcq.explanation: The FIN flag is sent to initiate an orderly, graceful shutdown of a half-close connection after pending data is flushed. The RST (Reset) flag immediately and forcefully tears down an invalid or rejected connection.

coding_mcq.title: ICMP Protocol Function
coding_mcq.question: Which network diagnostic utilities rely directly on Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) echo request and echo reply packets?
coding_mcq.explanation: The 'ping' utility sends ICMP Echo Request (Type 8) packets and expects ICMP Echo Reply (Type 0) packets. 'traceroute' also leverages ICMP Time Exceeded messages to discover router hops.

coding_mcq.title: SQL Aggregate Functions and NULL
coding_mcq.question: How do standard SQL aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT(column)) treat NULL values?
options: They throw a runtime SQL error
They automatically ignore/exclude NULL values during computation
They return NULL if any single row contains NULL
coding_mcq.explanation: In SQL, aggregate functions (SUM, AVG, COUNT(col), MIN, MAX) ignore NULL rows completely. (Note that COUNT(*) counts total rows including rows with NULLs, but COUNT(column_name) ignores NULLs).

coding_mcq.title: Clustered vs Non-Clustered Index
coding_mcq.question: How many Clustered Indexes can exist on a single relational database table, and why?
options: Exactly 1, because a clustered index physically dictates the physical storage order of rows on disk
None unless explicitly enabled in database configuration
coding_mcq.explanation: A clustered index determines the physical on-disk storage order of data rows. Since table data can only be physically ordered in one way on disk, only ONE clustered index can exist per table.

coding_mcq.title: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
coding_mcq.question: What is the core principle of Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) in database systems?
options: Data pages must be written to disk before the log is updated
Log records describing changes must be flushed to persistent disk storage BEFORE the corresponding dirty data pages are written to the database files
Logs are only written once a day in batch jobs
Writing logs asynchronously without disk synchronization
coding_mcq.explanation: WAL dictates that before any modified (dirty) data page is written to database disk storage, the log record describing the modification must be safely committed to non-volatile disk. This guarantees durability and crash recovery (ARIES).

coding_mcq.title: Database Deadlock Detection - Wait-For Graph
coding_mcq.question: In database transaction management, how is a deadlock detected using a Wait-For Graph (WFG)?
options: By checking if the number of edges exceeds the number of nodes
By detecting the presence of a directed cycle in the graph
By finding the minimum spanning tree of transactions
coding_mcq.explanation: In a Wait-For Graph where vertices represent active transactions and directed edges (Ti -> Tj) represent Ti waiting for a resource held by Tj, a deadlock exists if and only if the graph contains a directed cycle.

coding_mcq.title: SQL TRUNCATE vs DELETE
coding_mcq.question: What is a primary distinction between TRUNCATE TABLE and DELETE FROM table in SQL?
options: DELETE is a DDL operation while TRUNCATE is DML
TRUNCATE is a DDL operation that deallocates data pages quickly with minimal logging and resets identity counters, while DELETE is a DML operation that logs row-by-row deletions
TRUNCATE allows a WHERE clause while DELETE does not
TRUNCATE fires all row-level DELETE triggers
coding_mcq.explanation: TRUNCATE is a DDL command that deallocates the table's data pages, cannot have a WHERE clause, does not fire row triggers, and is much faster. DELETE is a DML command that removes rows one-by-one and logs each deletion.

coding_mcq.title: Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
coding_mcq.question: What does the Liskov Substitution Principle (the 'L' in SOLID) dictate?
options: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering the correctness of the program
Classes should only depend on concrete implementations
A class should have only one reason to change
Interfaces must be segregated into single-method contracts
coding_mcq.explanation: LSP states that objects of a superclass should be replaceable with objects of a subclass without affecting the correctness or expected behavior of the program. Subclasses must uphold the contracts and invariants of the parent.

coding_mcq.title: Composition over Inheritance
coding_mcq.question: Why is 'Composition over Inheritance' widely recommended in modern object-oriented software engineering?
options: Inheritance breaks encapsulation by tightly coupling subclasses to parent implementation details, whereas composition provides looser coupling and dynamic run-time behavior switching
Composition uses less memory than inheritance in all languages
Inheritance is completely unsupported in modern languages
coding_mcq.explanation: Inheritance exposes child classes to the fragile base class problem and tight compile-time coupling. Composition ('has-a') encapsulates behavior in separate components that can be changed or mocked at runtime.

coding_mcq.title: Shallow Copy vs Deep Copy
coding_mcq.question: What is the difference between a Shallow Copy and a Deep Copy of an object containing nested references?
options: A shallow copy duplicates primitive fields and copies references to nested objects, whereas a deep copy recursively clones the entire object graph so copies are completely independent
A shallow copy creates a database backup
A deep copy only copies static variables
A shallow copy creates new memory allocations for nested objects
coding_mcq.explanation: A shallow copy copies reference pointers, so modifying an inner nested object in the copy mutates the original. A deep copy recursively duplicates every referenced object in separate memory.

coding_mcq.title: Garbage Collection - Mark and Sweep
coding_mcq.question: How does the classic 'Mark and Sweep' garbage collection algorithm reclaim unused heap memory?
options: It counts references and deletes an object when its counter reaches zero
Phase 1 traverses from GC roots marking all reachable objects; Phase 2 scans the heap reclaiming unvisited, unmarked memory
It restarts the operating system process
It moves all objects to disk memory
coding_mcq.explanation: Mark and Sweep avoids reference counting circular reference leaks by: 1) Starting from GC roots (local stack variables, static fields) and marking all reachable objects, then 2) Sweeping the heap to free memory occupied by all unmarked objects.

coding_mcq.title: Factory Pattern vs Abstract Factory Pattern
coding_mcq.question: What is the distinction between the Factory Method pattern and the Abstract Factory pattern?
options: Factory Method creates a single product via inheritance, while Abstract Factory provides an interface to create families of related or dependent objects without specifying concrete classes
Factory Method is only used in C++, Abstract Factory only in Java
coding_mcq.explanation: Factory Method uses a single method to instantiate one product type (delegated to subclasses). Abstract Factory defines an interface for creating suites of related products (e.g., MacButton + MacCheckbox vs WinButton + WinCheckbox).

coding_mcq.title: Prefix Sum Array Query
coding_mcq.question: Given an array of size N, what is the time complexity to calculate the sum of elements between any two indices [L, R] using a precomputed Prefix Sum Array?
coding_mcq.explanation: A Prefix Sum array allows any range sum [L, R] to be answered in O(1) time using prefix[R] - prefix[L - 1].

coding_mcq.title: Disjoint Set Union (DSU) Path Compression
coding_mcq.question: What is the nearly-constant amortized time complexity per operation in a Disjoint Set Union (DSU) data structure using both Path Compression and Union by Rank?
coding_mcq.explanation: Using path compression and union by rank yields an amortized time per operation of O(alpha(N)), where alpha is the inverse Ackermann function, which is <= 4 for any practical input size.

coding_mcq.title: Segment Tree Range Query
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity to query a range sum or range minimum over N elements using a Segment Tree?
coding_mcq.explanation: A Segment Tree answers range queries in O(log N) time because at each level of the tree at most a constant number of nodes are visited.

coding_mcq.title: LRU Cache Data Structure Combination
coding_mcq.question: Which pair of data structures is classically used together to achieve O(1) get() and put() in a Least Recently Used (LRU) Cache?
coding_mcq.explanation: A Hash Map provides O(1) node lookup by key, and a Doubly Linked List allows O(1) node removal and insertion at the head (most recently used).

coding_mcq.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree) Update
coding_mcq.question: What is the time complexity to update an element and query prefix sums in a Binary Indexed Tree (Fenwick Tree) with N elements?
coding_mcq.explanation: A Fenwick Tree updates an element and queries prefix sums in O(log N) time by isolating the least significant bit (LSB) using `i += i & (-i)`.

coding_mcq.title: Page Replacement: LRU Approximation (Second Chance)
coding_mcq.question: The 'Second Chance' (Clock) page replacement algorithm uses which hardware bit in the page table entry to approximate LRU?
coding_mcq.explanation: The Clock algorithm inspects the Reference bit. If it is 1, it resets it to 0 and gives the page a second chance. If it is 0, the page is selected for replacement.

coding_mcq.title: Copy-On-Write (COW) in fork()
coding_mcq.question: How does Copy-on-Write (COW) optimize process creation during the fork() system call in modern operating systems?
options: Child and parent share the same physical pages marked read-only; a private physical copy is allocated only when either process attempts to write
It delays child execution until the parent exits
It compresses memory pages onto the swap partition
It duplicates all heap memory upfront
coding_mcq.explanation: Copy-On-Write avoids duplicating physical memory pages when fork() is called. Both parent and child share the pages read-only until one writes to a page, at which point the kernel creates an independent copy of only that page.

coding_mcq.title: Direct Memory Access (DMA)
coding_mcq.question: What is the primary architectural advantage of Direct Memory Access (DMA) during high-throughput I/O transfers?
options: Device controllers transfer blocks of data directly to/from main memory without continuous CPU intervention
It replaces physical RAM with high-speed registers
It eliminates the need for device drivers
coding_mcq.explanation: DMA allows I/O devices (like network cards and NVMe drives) to transfer data directly into system memory, interrupting the CPU only when the entire multi-kilobyte transfer block is complete.

coding_mcq.title: Internal vs External Fragmentation
coding_mcq.question: What is the fundamental difference between Internal Fragmentation and External Fragmentation in memory allocation?
options: Internal fragmentation is allocated memory that remains unused inside a partition; External fragmentation is free memory distributed in non-contiguous fragments outside allocated partitions
Internal fragmentation only occurs with virtual memory; external fragmentation only occurs in CPU caches
Internal fragmentation can be resolved by compaction; external cannot
coding_mcq.explanation: Internal fragmentation occurs when allocated fixed-size memory blocks (e.g. 4KB pages) are larger than requested. External fragmentation occurs when total free memory is sufficient to satisfy a request, but it is divided into non-contiguous slices.

coding_mcq.title: Priority Inversion and Priority Inheritance
coding_mcq.question: How does the 'Priority Inheritance' protocol resolve the Priority Inversion problem in real-time operating systems?
options: A lower-priority task holding a resource temporarily inherits the higher priority of a waiting task until it releases the resource
All tasks are assigned equal priority
High-priority tasks are placed in sleep mode
coding_mcq.explanation: Priority Inheritance temporarily raises the priority of the low-priority thread holding a critical lock to the priority of the highest-priority thread waiting on that lock, preventing intermediate-priority threads from starving the high-priority task.

coding_mcq.title: BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) Classification
coding_mcq.question: Which type of routing protocol is the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) utilized across the global Internet backbone?
coding_mcq.explanation: BGP is an exterior Path-Vector routing protocol used to exchange routing and reachability information between autonomous systems (AS) on the global Internet.

coding_mcq.title: Nagle's Algorithm
coding_mcq.question: What is the primary purpose of Nagle's Algorithm in TCP implementations?
options: Combining multiple small outgoing messages into a single TCP segment to prevent congesting the network with tiny packets (small-packet problem)
Increasing the initial congestion window to 100 MSS
coding_mcq.explanation: Nagle's algorithm buffers small outgoing data buffers and delays sending until an acknowledgment for previous data is received or until enough data accumulates to fill a full MSS segment, preventing 'tinygram' network congestion.

coding_mcq.title: HTTP/2 Multiplexing
coding_mcq.question: What major advancement in HTTP/2 eliminated the HTTP/1.1 Head-of-Line (HoL) blocking at the application layer?
options: Multiplexing multiple bidirectional streams concurrently over a single TCP connection
coding_mcq.explanation: HTTP/2 introduces binary framing and stream multiplexing, allowing multiple interleaved requests and responses to share a single underlying TCP connection without waiting for prior requests to complete.

coding_mcq.title: Network Address Translation (NAT)
coding_mcq.question: How does Port Address Translation (PAT / NAT Overload) allow hundreds of internal devices to share a single public IPv4 address?
options: By assigning each internal session a unique source port number on the public IP address
By rotating the public IP every 10 seconds
By converting IPv4 to IPv6 internally
By using MAC addresses over the Internet
coding_mcq.explanation: PAT (NAT Overload) maps private IP + private port combinations to a single public IP address using distinct public port numbers, tracking outbound sessions in a translation table.

coding_mcq.title: SYN Flood Attack Mitigation
coding_mcq.question: Which technique is commonly deployed on network servers to defend against TCP SYN Flood Denial-of-Service attacks without allocating memory state for half-open connections?
coding_mcq.explanation: SYN Cookies encode the connection parameters into the initial sequence number of the SYN-ACK packet. The server allocates no state until the client returns the final ACK containing the validated cookie.

coding_mcq.title: Phantom Read Anomaly
coding_mcq.question: What constitutes a 'Phantom Read' anomaly in a database transaction?
options: A transaction re-executes a range query and discovers new rows inserted and committed by another transaction matching the filter criteria
Reading uncommitted data that is later rolled back
Reading modified columns in the same row with different values
A database crash during index updates
coding_mcq.explanation: A Phantom Read occurs when transaction T1 executes a query with a search condition (e.g., WHERE age > 30), and transaction T2 inserts new rows satisfying the condition and commits. When T1 reruns the query, it sees newly appeared 'phantom' rows.

coding_mcq.title: Database Star Schema vs Snowflake Schema
coding_mcq.question: What is the distinguishing difference between a Star Schema and a Snowflake Schema in data warehousing?
options: In a Snowflake Schema, dimension tables are normalized into multiple related tables, whereas in a Star Schema, dimension tables are completely denormalized
A Star Schema has no central fact table
A Snowflake Schema cannot store numeric metrics
A Star Schema uses B-Trees while a Snowflake schema uses hash tables
coding_mcq.explanation: In a Star Schema, dimensions are completely denormalized around a central fact table. In a Snowflake Schema, dimension tables are normalized into multiple related tables, reducing redundancy at the cost of more complex join queries.

coding_mcq.title: SQL Window Functions vs Aggregate Functions
coding_mcq.question: How do SQL Window Functions (e.g. ROW_NUMBER(), RANK(), OVER(PARTITION BY...)) differ from traditional GROUP BY aggregations?
options: Window functions compute values over a set of rows while preserving each individual row in the output, whereas GROUP BY collapses rows into a single summary row
Window functions can only run on temporary tables
Window functions cannot calculate averages or sums
GROUP BY cannot use numeric columns
coding_mcq.explanation: Unlike GROUP BY which collapses multiple rows into a single aggregated row, SQL window functions calculate calculations across related rows (the window) while keeping individual rows intact.

coding_mcq.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)
coding_mcq.question: Under which condition does Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) outperform pessimistic locking mechanisms in database transactions?
options: In environments with low data contention where transaction conflicts are rare
In write-heavy systems with frequent concurrent writes to the same row
When disk storage is almost full
When transactions run for several hours
coding_mcq.explanation: OCC executes transactions without acquiring locks, validating data versioning before commit. It provides superior throughput when data contention is low because transactions never block each other waiting for locks.

coding_mcq.title: Composite Index Column Ordering
coding_mcq.question: Given a composite index on (Department, HireDate), which SQL query can utilize this index efficiently (the Leftmost Prefix rule)?
coding_mcq.explanation: A B-Tree composite index on (A, B) requires queries to filter on the leftmost column 'A' in order to traverse the tree. Filtering only on 'B' without 'A' cannot use the index hierarchy and requires a full table scan.

coding_mcq.title: TCP Window Size and Flow Control
coding_mcq.question: What is the purpose of the 'Receive Window' (rwnd) field in the TCP header?
options: It advertises the number of bytes the receiver is currently willing and able to accept to prevent buffer overflow
It specifies the maximum packet hop limit
coding_mcq.explanation: The TCP Receive Window field implements end-to-end flow control, informing the sender how much free buffer space the receiver currently has.

coding_mcq.title: Process Scheduling: Round Robin Quantum
coding_mcq.question: In Round Robin CPU scheduling, what happens if the time quantum is set to an extremely large value (larger than the longest process burst)?
options: The scheduling algorithm behaves exactly like First-Come, First-Served (FCFS)
It becomes Shortest Remaining Time First
coding_mcq.explanation: If the time quantum is larger than any job's burst time, each job runs to completion without preemption, which is equivalent to FCFS.

coding_mcq.title: Hashing: Separate Chaining vs Open Addressing
coding_mcq.question: What is the load factor (lambda) threshold typically used in Java's HashMap before resizing and rehashing occurs?
coding_mcq.explanation: Java's HashMap uses a default load factor of 0.75, which offers a proven trade-off between time complexity and memory overhead before doubling capacity.

coding_mcq.title: Relational Database Foreign Key Constraint
coding_mcq.question: What does the 'ON DELETE CASCADE' clause on a foreign key constraint do when a referenced row in the parent table is deleted?
options: It automatically deletes all corresponding child rows referencing the deleted parent row
It sets the child foreign key values to NULL
It prevents the parent row from being deleted
It raises an unhandled database exception
coding_mcq.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE ensures referential integrity by automatically propagating the deletion to any child rows that reference the deleted primary key.

coding_mcq.title: Inheritance: Diamond Problem in Java

options: To prevent ambiguity and complexity arising from the Diamond Problem (conflicting method implementations)
Because Java has no garbage collection for multiple classes
To speed up execution of static variables
coding_mcq.explanation: Java disallows multiple class inheritance to avoid the ambiguity of inheriting duplicate method implementations with the same signature from multiple parents.
